blocks.text: A rugby player lands on his outstretched arm and the round contour of his shoulder suddenly flattens, with a hollow beneath the acromion. The same joint that lets you throw a ball, scratch your back and hang from a bar is the most commonly dislocated large joint in the body. The reason lies in its bones and in what holds them together.

blocks.markdown: The **shoulder girdle** (pectoral girdle) consists of the **clavicle** and **scapula** on each side. It links the upper limb to the axial skeleton, at the **sternoclavicular joint** (the only bony attachment to the trunk), and carries the **glenohumeral joint** where the humerus meets the scapula. Understanding the shoulder means knowing the landmarks of these three bones, the muscles that move and stabilise them, and the compromise the joint makes between mobility and stability.

blocks.title: Glenohumeral joint
blocks.text: A synovial ball-and-socket joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The glenoid is shallow and is deepened slightly by a rim of fibrocartilage, the glenoid labrum. The joint is surrounded by a thin, lax fibrous capsule and has the greatest range of movement of any joint in the body.

rows: Sternal end, acromial end, S-shaped shaft, conoid tubercle and trapezoid line (inferior surface, lateral third)
Strut holding the limb away from the trunk; most often broken at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. Coracoclavicular ligaments attach to the conoid tubercle and trapezoid line.
Acromion, spine, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles, suprascapular notch, subscapular, supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, inferior angle
Acromion articulates with the clavicle; coracoid is an attachment site for pectoralis minor, short head of biceps and coracobrachialis; glenoid is the socket.
Head, anatomical neck, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, intertubercular (bicipital) groove, surgical neck
Tubercles receive the rotator cuff tendons; the axillary nerve lies on the surgical neck; the long head of biceps runs in the intertubercular groove.
blocks.caption: Bony landmarks of the shoulder girdle.

blocks.markdown: **Using the landmarks.** The **spine of the scapula** divides the posterior surface into the supraspinous fossa above (supraspinatus) and the infraspinous fossa below (infraspinatus), and it ends laterally as the acromion. The **suprascapular notch** on the superior border, beside the base of the coracoid, is crossed by the suprascapular nerve, which is why a lesion there weakens both supraspinatus and infraspinatus. The **supraglenoid tubercle** (above the glenoid) gives origin to the long head of biceps brachii and the **infraglenoid tubercle** (below it) to the long head of triceps brachii. On the humerus the **greater** and **lesser tubercles** are separated by the **intertubercular (bicipital) groove**, in which the tendon of the long head of biceps runs; the **surgical neck**, below the tubercles, is the common fracture site and lies against the axillary nerve.

**Joints of the girdle.** At the **acromioclavicular joint** the acromial end of the clavicle meets the acromion; stability comes mainly from the **coracoclavicular ligament**, which has a medial **conoid** part and a lateral **trapezoid** part passing from the coracoid process to the clavicle. At the **sternoclavicular joint** the medial end of the clavicle meets the manubrium and first costal cartilage. The scapula also glides across the posterior thoracic wall (the scapulothoracic articulation, a physiological rather than synovial joint) to position the glenoid.

blocks.title: Scapulohumeral rhythm
blocks.prompt: In full abduction the movement is shared between the glenohumeral joint and the scapulothoracic joint in an approximate 2:1 ratio (glenohumeral : scapular rotation). If the arm is abducted through a total of 150 degrees, how much occurs at the glenohumeral joint?

steps.text: Write the ratio as 2 parts glenohumeral to 1 part scapular, so the total is 3 parts.
Glenohumeral movement is 2 parts: 2 x 50 = 100 degrees; scapular rotation is 1 part: 50 degrees.

blocks.answer: 100 degrees at the glenohumeral joint (and 50 degrees of scapular rotation).

blocks.markdown: **The rotator cuff.** Four short muscles arise from the scapula and insert by flattened tendons on the tubercles of the humeral head. They fuse with the capsule and act as dynamic stabilisers that hold the humeral head in the glenoid. Use the mnemonic **SITS**:

rows: Initiates abduction (first 15 degrees), then assists deltoid
Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5, C6)
blocks.caption: The rotator cuff (SITS). The tendons of supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis alone inserts on the lesser tubercle.

blocks.title: Mobility at the price of stability
blocks.text: The humeral head is about three to four times larger in articular area than the shallow glenoid, the capsule is lax, and there is little bony restraint. Stability therefore depends mostly on soft tissues: the rotator cuff tendons, the glenoid labrum, the glenohumeral ligaments and the long head of biceps. Above, the joint is protected by the coracoacromial arch (acromion, coracoacromial ligament and coracoid). Inferiorly there is no muscle or ligament support, so the weakest point is the inferior capsule.

blocks.markdown: **Why dislocation happens.** Most dislocations (about 95 percent, a widely quoted figure) are **anterior**, typically when the abducted arm is forced into lateral rotation. The head slips out through the weak anteroinferior capsule and comes to lie in front of the glenoid, below the coracoid process. The nearby **axillary nerve**, which winds around the **surgical neck** of the humerus, is at risk, causing numbness over the lower deltoid ('regimental badge' area) and weak abduction. Rotator cuff tears and subacromial impingement are other common pathologies: the supraspinatus tendon runs under the acromion and coracoacromial ligament, so it can be pinched when the arm is abducted. This causes a 'painful arc' in the middle range (approximately 60 to 120 degrees) of abduction.

blocks.title: Which rotator cuff muscle is torn?
blocks.prompt: A patient cannot start to abduct the arm from the side, but once the arm is passively lifted a few degrees, deltoid can continue the movement. Lateral rotation strength is normal. Which muscle is most likely damaged, and which nerve supplies it?

steps.text: Initiation of abduction in the first 15 degrees is the role of supraspinatus; deltoid takes over thereafter.

Normal lateral rotation means infraspinatus is intact, so a suprascapular nerve lesion at the suprascapular notch (which would affect both supraspinatus and infraspinatus) is unlikely; the most likely lesion is a supraspinatus tendon tear.
Supraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, which passes through the suprascapular notch.

blocks.answer: Supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve, C5 and C6); a tear of its tendon would explain failure to initiate abduction.

items: SITS: Supraspinatus (abduction), Infraspinatus and Teres minor (lateral rotation), Subscapularis (medial rotation).
Greater tubercle receives three tendons; lesser tubercle receives one.
Anterior dislocation is commonest because the joint is weakest anteroinferiorly.
Axillary nerve at the surgical neck is vulnerable in dislocation and in fracture of the surgical neck.

blocks.title: Labrum versus capsule
blocks.text: The glenoid labrum deepens the socket (increasing its depth) but does not replace the capsule. Remember that the thinnest, weakest part of the capsule is inferior, which is why dislocation is anteroinferior.

points: The pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula) attaches the limb to the trunk at the sternoclavicular joint; the glenohumeral joint is a shallow ball-and-socket joint.

The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) dynamically stabilises the joint; supraspinatus initiates abduction, infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate, subscapularis medially rotates.
The joint's large range of motion comes at the cost of stability, so anteroinferior dislocation is common and can injure the axillary nerve.

questions.stem: The conoid tubercle on the inferior surface of the clavicle gives attachment to which ligament?

options.text: Conoid part of the coracoclavicular ligament

questions.correctOptionText: Conoid part of the coracoclavicular ligament

distractorRationale.b: Glenohumeral ligaments are capsular thickenings attaching to the humerus and glenoid, not the clavicle.
distractorRationale.c: The coracoacromial ligament runs between the coracoid and the acromion.
distractorRationale.d: The transverse humeral ligament bridges the intertubercular groove.

questions.explanation: The coracoclavicular ligament joins the coracoid process to the inferior surface of the clavicle; its conoid part attaches to the conoid tubercle and the trapezoid part to the trapezoid line. This ligament is the main stabiliser of the acromioclavicular joint.

questions.stem: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus?

distractorRationale.a: Supraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle.
distractorRationale.b: Infraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle.
distractorRationale.c: Teres minor inserts on the greater tubercle.

questions.explanation: Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle inserting on the lesser tubercle, and it medially rotates the arm. The other three tendons insert on the greater tubercle.

questions.stem: Which muscle initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction at the shoulder?

distractorRationale.a: Deltoid continues abduction after supraspinatus has started it.

questions.explanation: Supraspinatus lies above the scapular spine and passes over the top of the joint, so it begins abduction before deltoid takes over. Because it is the initiator, an injury to its tendon or to the suprascapular nerve prevents the movement starting.

questions.stem: Assume that abduction of the arm divides between the glenohumeral joint and scapular rotation in a 2:1 ratio. During an abduction of 120 degrees overall, how many degrees occur at the glenohumeral joint? Give your answer in degrees.
questions.explanation: A 2:1 ratio means the total is 3 parts, so each part is 120 divided by 3, which is 40 degrees. The glenohumeral joint contributes 2 parts, which is 80 degrees, and the scapula rotates through the remaining 40 degrees.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old painter has shoulder pain only between about 60 and 120 degrees of abduction, with pain relief once the arm is fully raised. Which structure is most likely being compressed beneath the coracoacromial arch?

distractorRationale.b: Subscapularis lies anterior to the joint and does not pass under the acromion.
distractorRationale.c: The axillary nerve runs beneath the deltoid at the surgical neck, not under the coracoacromial arch.
distractorRationale.d: The labrum lies within the joint on the glenoid rim.

questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion and coracoacromial ligament, and is pinched during mid-range abduction, causing a painful arc. Beyond about 120 degrees the tendon has moved clear, which is why pain eases.

questions.stem: Which feature best explains why the shoulder dislocates most often anteroinferiorly?

options.text: The inferior part of the capsule is weak and has no rotator cuff support
The glenoid cavity is deep and faces posteriorly
The coracoacromial arch lies below the joint
The humeral head is smaller than the glenoid

questions.correctOptionText: The inferior part of the capsule is weak and has no rotator cuff support

distractorRationale.b: The glenoid is shallow, not deep.
distractorRationale.c: The coracoacromial arch lies above the joint and prevents upward displacement.
distractorRationale.d: The humeral head is larger in articular area than the glenoid.

questions.explanation: The rotator cuff and the coracoacromial arch protect the joint superiorly, anteriorly and posteriorly, but the inferior capsule is thin and unsupported by any cuff muscle. A force on the abducted, laterally rotated arm therefore drives the head out through that weak inferior part.

questions.stem: Which scapular landmark is crossed by the suprascapular nerve on its way to supraspinatus and infraspinatus?

distractorRationale.b: The infraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the long head of triceps.
distractorRationale.c: The inferior angle is the lowest point of the scapula and has no nerve crossing it.
distractorRationale.d: The subscapular fossa is the anterior surface where subscapularis arises.

questions.explanation: The suprascapular notch lies on the superior border of the scapula beside the coracoid process, and the suprascapular nerve passes through it. A lesion at this notch therefore weakens both supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

questions.stem: A radiograph shows a fracture just below the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. Which statement about the neighbouring landmarks is correct?

options.text: The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular groove, which holds the tendon of the long head of biceps
The tubercles are separated by the suprascapular notch, which holds the axillary nerve
The fracture is through the anatomical neck, which lies below the tubercles
The lesser tubercle receives the tendon of infraspinatus

questions.correctOptionText: The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular groove, which holds the tendon of the long head of biceps

distractorRationale.b: The suprascapular notch is on the scapula, not the humerus.
distractorRationale.c: The anatomical neck lies at the junction of the head and the tubercles, above them; the fracture described is at the surgical neck.
distractorRationale.d: Infraspinatus inserts on the greater tubercle; the lesser tubercle receives subscapularis.

questions.explanation: The greater and lesser tubercles flank the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which carries the tendon of the long head of biceps. A fracture just below the tubercles is at the surgical neck, where the axillary nerve lies close to the bone.

questions.stem: Name the four rotator cuff muscles, state the action of each, and state which nerve supplies each.
markingGuide: Teres minor: lateral rotation; axillary nerve.
Subscapularis: medial rotation; upper and lower subscapular nerves.
Mention that all four tendons blend with the joint capsule and stabilise the head in the glenoid.
questions.explanation: The SITS mnemonic gives the four muscles, and they share the common role of dynamically holding the humeral head in the glenoid. Knowing the individual nerve supply lets you localise lesions of the suprascapular, axillary or subscapular nerves.

questions.stem: Explain why the glenohumeral joint has a very large range of movement but is prone to dislocation, and describe the structures that provide stability and the nerve at risk in anterior dislocation.
markingGuide: Shallow glenoid cavity and a much larger humeral head give little bony constraint.
Thin, lax capsule allows a large range of movement.
Stability from the rotator cuff, glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments and the long head of biceps.
Coracoacromial arch protects superiorly; inferior capsule is weakest, with no cuff support.
The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck and may be stretched or injured, causing lower deltoid numbness and weak abduction.
questions.explanation: Mobility and stability pull against each other in a ball-and-socket joint with such a small socket, so soft tissues take the stabilising role. When these fail inferiorly the head dislocates and endangers the axillary nerve lying just below.
